title: Atmospheric channel model for QKD over satellite megaconstellations
authors: Sergio Gándara Gándara, Javier Vecino-Peñas, Ana Fernández-Vilas, Manuel Fernández-Veiga, Rebeca P. Díaz-Redondo
abstract: Atmospheric turbulence and channel loss represent the primary limiting factors in ground-to-satellite quantum communication systems, yet their joint impact remains insufficiently characterized across diverse operational conditions. In this work, we develop a comprehensive and open atmospheric channel model for quantum optical links along ground-to-satellite paths, integrating altitude-dependent molecular and aerosol absorptions. The model is validated with available data from missions such as Micius and Hispasat, including a secondary viability assessment for a hypothetical Starlink-based quantum communication network, where we evaluate the predicted channel behavior in terms of single-photon transmittance and power balance, alongside the channel capacity of the link for uplink and downlink exclusively. Our comparative analysis demonstrates the ability of our channel model to predict real data under simple atmospheric behavior assumptions, which offer practical guidelines for the design and optimization of future quantum satellite missions.
summary: This paper presents a comprehensive atmospheric channel model to quantify signal loss for quantum key distribution (QKD) over ground-to-satellite links. By integrating detailed atmospheric physics, the authors predict key performance indicators like secure key rate and QBER. The results validate the model against real mission data, providing crucial guidelines for future quantum satellite network design.
main_problem: The primary challenge is accurately characterizing the joint impact of atmospheric turbulence and channel loss on quantum communication links between ground stations and orbiting satellites.
main_result: The developed model successfully predicts quantum key distribution (QKD) performance metrics, such as the secure key rate and QBER, showing numerical consistency with established results from missions like Micius.
method: The authors developed a comprehensive atmospheric channel model that integrates altitude-dependent molecular and aerosol absorptions, alongside modeling depolarization effects using master equations.
model_or_system: The system is a quantum optical link traversing the Earth's atmosphere from a ground station to a satellite. The model incorporates five atmospheric layers (Troposphere to Exosphere) and calculates atmospheric attenuation and refractive index changes.
key_observables: Single-photon transmittance, power balance, channel capacity, Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER), and Secure Key Rate (SKR).
important_parameters: Atmospheric altitude (z), wavelength (e.g., 1550 nm), and elevation angle ($	heta$).
main_assumptions: The model assumes atmospheric gasses behave as ideal gasses, and the Starlink assessment relies on using Micius specifications due to a lack of direct data.
figures_summary: Figures show Pressure and Temperature profiles across atmospheric layers, refractive indices vs. altitude, and atmospheric transmissivity/power vs. elevation angles for satellite links.
paper_structure: The paper first develops the atmospheric channel model by calculating gas densities and refractive index. It then models intensity loss (absorption/scattering) and depolarization. Finally, it applies this framework to simulate QKD performance (SKR and QBER) for both existing and hypothetical megaconstellation links.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the physical channel impairments (absorption, scattering, turbulence) that limit the practical implementation of quantum communication networks, which is a critical engineering and theoretical hurdle for quantum information science.
